# Introduction

This project was developed for the Programming in Psychological Science course at the University of Amsterdam.

The project investigates psychological data and aims to combine data exploration, statistical analyses, visualisations, and an interactive component.

# Dataset

The dataset (Mentalillness.csv, Kaggle) contains 3,753 synthetic participants
with 53 binary DSM-5 symptoms and criteria (0 = absent, 1 = present) and 5
binary diagnoses: bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, depression, anxiety
disorder, and PTSD. It is stored in the `data` folder.

Because the original column names are long, we first build a variable key that
gives each column a short name and records which disorder and DSM-5 criterion
it belongs to. The key is saved as `data/variable_key.csv`. We then load the
data with these short names and check that every value is 0 or 1.

```{r load-data}
source("src/r/functions_data.R")
source("src/r/functions_variable_key.R")

variable_key <- make_variable_key()
save_variable_key(variable_key, "data/variable_key.csv")
clindata <- load_mental_illness("data/Mentalillness.csv", variable_key)

knitr::kable(head(variable_key, 10))
```

## DSM rules

The diagnoses in the dataset follow fixed counting rules. The script
`test_dsm_rules.R` rebuilds all five diagnoses from the symptom columns
(with `apply_dsm_rules()`) and checks them in two ways.

```{r dsm-checks, include = FALSE}
source("src/r/test_dsm_rules.R")
```

First, it checks that the rebuilt diagnoses match the diagnoses in the data
for every participant.

```{r dsm-rule-check}
knitr::kable(rule_check)
```

### Tests

Second, it tests the rules on made-up participants placed exactly at a
cutoff (or just below it), whose diagnosis we know in advance. This is where
mistakes like `>` instead of `>=` would show up.

```{r dsm-tests}
knitr::kable(test_results)
```

# Statistical analysis

The script `analyses.R` runs the tests and `plots.R` makes the figures.

```{r analyses, include = FALSE}
source("src/r/analyses.R")
source("src/r/plots.R")
```

## Worked example

To show how each test works, we tested whether depressed mood was significantly associated with a depression diagnosis. A chi-square test of independence compares the observed counts with the counts expected under independence; phi (φ) gives the effect size.

```{r worked-example}
example_table
example_test
round(example_phi, 3)
```

Depressed mood was significantly associated with a depression diagnosis, χ²(1) = 284.84,
p < .001, φ = .28.

## Symptoms and diagnoses

We repeated this test for every symptom against every diagnosis
(53 × 5 = 265 tests). P-values were corrected for multiple testing with the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR, q < .05).

```{r symptom-summary}
knitr::kable(association_summary)
```

```{r symptom-heatmap, fig.height = 10, fig.width = 7}
heatmap_plot
```

After FDR correction, 37 of 53 symptoms were significantly associated with their own diagnosis (φ up to .90). None of the 212 symptom–other-diagnosis pairs were significant (φ = -.04 to .05). This patter is consistent with each diagnosis being determined only by its own symptoms. All 16 non-significant within-disorder association involved PTSD symptoms (φ =< .05). Because PTSD requires all eight criteria to be met at once, so a single symptom barely changes the odds of the diagnosis.

## Comorbidity

For every pair of diagnoses, we used a chi-square test to compare the observed number of participants with diagnoses against the number of expected under independence. P-values were FDR-corrected across the 10 pairs. 

```{r comorbidity}
knitr::kable(comorbidity, digits = 3)
comorbidity_plot
```

Observed co-occurrence did not differ significantly from the expected value for any of the ten pairs (observed/expected ratios .86-1.15, all FDR-corrected p > .31). This contrasts with clinical data, where diagnoses typically co-occur more often than expected by chance. 

## Symptom count and diagnosis

```{r count-steps, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 8}
steps_plot
```

For bipolar and depression, the proportion diagnosed jumps from 0 to 1 exactly
at the cutoff. For anxiety it levels off at about .50, because the diagnosis
also requires the 6-month duration item, which about half of participants have. For
schizophrenia it rises gradually, because a positive symptom is also required.
The dip at 6 anxiety symptoms (.46) most likely reflects sampling variation in a small group (n = 66).
